extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, proofreaders, typesetters, and publishers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical rules and standards for hyphenation, word divisions, footnotes, indexing, tables, spacing, indentation, headings, and other typographical and editorial matters for book and journal composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation of by- compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of "by-" should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: by-product, by-laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation of co-, pre-, re- prefixes
rubrics_metrics.description: The prefixes "co-," "pre-," and "re-," when followed by the same vowel as that in which they terminate, take a hyphen; as a rule they do not when followed by a different vowel or by a consonant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: co-operation, pre-empted, re-enter; but: coequal, coeducation, prearranged, reinstal; cohabitation, prehistoric, recast (re-read). Note: Botanical Gazette prints cooperate, reenter. Exceptions include combinations with proper names, long or unusual formations, and words where omission of hyphen changes meaning (e.g., pie-Raphaelite; re-formation vs reformation; re-cover = cover again).

rubrics_metrics.name: No hyphen for certain common words
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the hyphen from 'today,' 'tomorrow,' 'tonight,' 'viewpoint,' 'standpoint.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See cross-reference to rule 119 for related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative particles un-, in-, a-
rubrics_metrics.description: The negative particles 'un-,' 'in-,' and 'a-' do not usually require a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: unmanly, undemocratic, inanimate, indeterminate, illimitable, impersonal, as3rmmetrical. Exceptions would be rare and artificial combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation with non-
rubrics_metrics.description: The particle 'non-' ordinarily calls for a hyphen, except in the commonest words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: non-aesthetic, non-subservient, non-contagious, non-ability, non-interference, non-unionist, non-membership; but: nonage, nondescript, nonessential, nonplus, nonsense, noncombatant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen with quasi-
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Quasi' prefixed to a noun or an adjective requires a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: quasi-corporation, quasi-historical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Over- and under- prefixes usually closed
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Over' and 'under' prefixed to a word should not be followed by a hyphen, except in rare cases (lengthy words, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: overbold, overemphasize, overweight, underfed, underestimate, undersecretary; but: over-soul, under-man, over-spiritualistic, over-search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin preposition prefixes no hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: The Latin prepositions 'ante,' 'anti,' 'inter,' 'intra,' 'post,' 'sub,' and 'super' prefixed to a word do not ordinarily require a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: antedate, antechamber, antediluvian, antidote, antiseptic (but: anti-imperialistic — cf. rule 203), international, interstate, intercity, intramural (but: intra-atomic), postscript, postgraduate, postprandial, subconscious, submarine, subtitle, subway, superfine. Exceptions: ante-bellum, ante-Nicene, anti-Semitic, inter-university, post-revolutionary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen with extra-, infra-, supra-, ultra-
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Extra,' 'infra,' 'supra,' and 'ultra' as a rule call for a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: extra-hazardous, infra-mundane, supra-temporal, ultra-conservative (but: Ultramontane).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation in spelled-out fractions
rubrics_metrics.description: In fractional numbers, spelled out, connect by a hyphen the numerator and the denominator, unless either already contains a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The year is two-thirds gone'; four and five-sevenths; thirty-hundredths; but: thirty-one hundredths. Do not hyphenate in constructions like 'One half of his fortune he bequeathed to his widow; the other, to charitable institutions.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Elliptical compounds indicated by hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: When two or more compound words occurring together have one component element in common which is omitted from all but the last word, indicate its implication by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in English- and German-speaking countries; one-, five-, and ten-cent pieces; 'in fifth- and tenth-century Europe' (quote). Note: Some writers regard this hyphen as an objectionable Teutonism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen to indicate incomplete prefix or suffix
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is used to indicate a prefix or a suffix, as a particle or syllable, not complete in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The prefix a-'; 'The German diminutive suffixes -chen and -few.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen to indicate syllables
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is employed to indicate the syllables of a word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: di-a-gram, pho-tog-ra-phy.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of common hyphenated words
rubrics_metrics.description: A specified list of words of everyday occurrence which should be hyphenated and do not fall under earlier classifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes: after-years, cross-section, man-of-war, son-in-law, bas-relief, death-rate, object-lesson, subject-matter, birth-rate, feast-day, page-proof, thought-process, blood-feud, folk-song, pay-roll, title-page, blood-relations, food-stuff, poor-law, wave-length, common-sense, fountain-head, post-office, well-being, cross-examine, guinea-pig, sea-level, well-nigh, cross-reference, horse-power, sense-perception, will-power, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary word divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid all unnecessary divisions of words; wherever consistent with good spacing, carry the whole word over into the next line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good spacing is paramount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dividing very short syllables
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not, in wide measures (20 ems or more), divide on a syllable of two letters if possible; words of four letters should never be divided; words of five or six rarely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: avoid dividing 'only' as on-ly; 'occur' oc-cur is acceptable rarely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit consecutive hyphenated line endings
rubrics_metrics.description: Never let more than two consecutive lines terminate in a hyphen if avoidable; next-to-last line shouldn't end in a divided word; last line (breakline) in measures of 15 ems and up should contain at least four letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also try to avoid a divided word at the bottom of a right-hand (recto) page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not divide proper nouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not divide proper nouns, especially names of persons, unless absolutely necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to place and person names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep initials and abbreviations intact
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not separate the initials of a name, or combinations like A.D., P.M., etc., across lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep such sequences on one line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep divisional marks with the section
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid separation (putting in different lines) of a divisional mark (e.g., (a) or (i)) from the section which it precedes; carry it over with the matter to which it pertains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide words by pronunciation (American system)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide according to pronunciation (the American system), not according to derivation (the English system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: democ-racy not demo-cracy; knowl-edge not know-ledge; aurif-erous not auri-ferous; antip-odes (better: antipodes). Where compatible with pronunciation and good spacing, divide compounds on etymological lines (dis-pleasure better than displeas-ure; school-master better than schoolmas-ter). Avoid monstrosities like Passo-ver, diso-bedience, une-ven, disa-bled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division between two consonants
rubrics_metrics.description: When two consonants meet between vowels and the syllable ends on one consonant, the division may properly be made between the consonants, pronunciation determining the place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: advan-tage, exces-sive, finan-der, foun-da-tion, impor-tant, In-dian, moun-tain, profes-sor, struc-ture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid line termination in soft c or g and -ing separation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not terminate a line in a soft c or g, or in '-ing' if possible; prefer to carry present participle '-ing' over to following line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: pro-cess, not proc-ess; ne-cessary, not nec-essary; spacing, not spac-ing; pro-geny not prog-eny; pre-judice not prej-udice. Note: This rule differs from some dictionary practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide on a vowel when practicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide on a vowel wherever practicable; if a vowel alone forms a syllable in the middle of a word, run it into the first line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sepa-rate, not sep-arate; particu-lar, not partic-ular; criti-dsm (criticism) not crit-idsm. Exceptions: words in -able and -ible should carry the vowel into the next line: read-able, not reada-ble; convert-ible, not converti-ble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid additional hyphens in hyphenated compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: In hyphenated nouns and adjectives avoid additional hyphens when dividing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: object-lesson not object-les-son; fellow-being not fel-low-being; poverty-stricken not pov-erty-stricken or pover-ty-stricken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not divide diphthongs
rubrics_metrics.description: A coalition of two vowel-sounds into one (a diphthong) should be treated as one letter; therefore do not divide if there is any escape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: peo-ple (either syllable makes a bad division), Cae-sar (Caesar), ail-ing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division in derivatives with accent shift
rubrics_metrics.description: In derivatives from words ending in -t (or other specific letters), the final consonant in divisions should be carried into the next line with the suffix if the accent has shifted; if the derivative retained the accent of the parent word, the consonant should be left in the first line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: objec-tive (from ob'ject); defect-ive (from defect').

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural -s does not justify new division
rubrics_metrics.description: The addition of a plural 's' adding a new syllable to words ending in an -s sound does not create an excuse for dividing such words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: dividing 'horses' or 'circumstances' so as to make 'hor-ses' or 'drcumstan-ces' is impossible/incorrect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of adjectives in -ical
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives in -ical (rendered in text as '-deal' likely meaning '-ical') should be divided on the 'i' (i.e., physi-cal), not phys-ical or physic-al.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: physical, not phys-ical or physic-al.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not divide the word 'nothing'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not divide nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule appears as an admonition against nonsensical divisions (literal phrasing retained).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-language division — French (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: For French words, divide on a vowel as far as possible, avoiding consonantal ending of syllables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in-di-vi-si-bi-li-té, a-che-ter; tableau (not tab-leau); balancer (not bal-ancer).

rubrics_metrics.name: French: certain consonant clusters
rubrics_metrics.description: Two consonants of which the second is 't' or 'r' (but not combinations 'rl,' 'lr') are both carried over to the following syllable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ta-bleau, é-cri-vain, per-dre, qua-tre; par-ler, hur-ler.

rubrics_metrics.name: French: count syllables by vowels
rubrics_metrics.description: There are as many syllables as there are vowels, even if soundless; a mute 'e' following a vowel does not form a syllable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: par-lent, vic-toi-re, pro-pri-é-taire, guer-re, fil-les; but: é-taient, joue-rai. Also letters like i, y, o when preceding other vowels may act as consonants and not form a syllable: bien, tions, yeux, loin, fouetter, écouelle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-language division — German (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: For German, the fundamental principle is to divide on a vowel as far as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: hü-ten, le-ben, Fa-brik.

rubrics_metrics.name: German: consonant clusters between vowels
rubrics_metrics.description: If several consonants stand between vowels, usually only the last is carried over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Rit-ter, klir-ren, Klemp-ner, Ver-wand-te, Karp-fen.

rubrics_metrics.name: German: never separate certain clusters
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinations such as sz, ch, sch, phy, sty, tk, dltq (as rendered in text) (and specifically s before certain letters) are never separated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Busche, Be-cher, Hascher (but: Haus-chen), Geo-gra-phie, La-sten, Ma-thilde. (See full manual for exact clusters.)

rubrics_metrics.name: German: dividing ck
rubrics_metrics.description: If 'ck' must be divided, separate it into k-k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Deckel — Dek-kel.

rubrics_metrics.name: German: divisions in Fremdwörter and compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: In foreign words (Fremdwörter), certain consonant combinations are carried over; compound words are separated first into component elements, applying foregoing rules within each element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Pu-bli-kum, Me-trum, Hy-drant; Fürsten-schloss, Tür-an-gel, Inter-esse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-language division — Italian
rubrics_metrics.description: In Italian, divide on a vowel as far as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ta-vo-lo-no, nar-rà-re.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italian: never separate certain clusters
rubrics_metrics.description: Consonant clusters such as s before a consonant, r following a consonant, ch, gh, gli, qu, sc, etc., are never separated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ca-stf-ghi, avro, migliò-re, bi-sé-gno, in-chi-stro, usare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italian: semivowel behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: i=y and u=w go with the following vowel; certain vowel sequences are not separated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mièi, tuéi (rendered in text with diacritics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-language division — Spanish
rubrics_metrics.description: In Spanish, divide on a vowel as far as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ca-ra-co-les, flu-xi-ón, re-ba-no, fle-xi-bi-li-dad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spanish: treat certain digraphs as single consonants
rubrics_metrics.description: ch, ll, rr, ñ (rendered as 'chy U y' in text) are regarded as simple consonants; cc and nn are divided as in English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mu-cha-cho, ba-ta-lla, bu-llo, ba-rre-no, ci-ga-rro; ac-ce-so, ac-ci-on, en-no-ble-cer, in-ne-ga-ble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spanish: liquids with preceding consonant not separated
rubrics_metrics.description: Liquid consonants l and r, when preceded by any consonant other than s, must not be separated from that consonant, except in uniting parts of compound words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ha-blar, po-dria, ce-le-bra-don, si-glo; but sub-lu-nar, sub-ra-yar, es-la-bon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spanish: divide two separable consonants
rubrics_metrics.description: Two separable consonants should be divided; g is always disjoined from following consonant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: cuer-da, chas-co, pron-to; has-ta, as-pi-rar, cons-pi-rar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-language division — Greek: consonants
rubrics_metrics.description: Single consonants, combinations that can begin a word, and mutes followed by l or r are placed at the beginning of a syllable; other consonant combinations are divided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples are given in Greek script in the manual (preserve original syllabification rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek: compound words
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound words are divided into their original parts; within each part apply the foregoing Greek rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: compounds shown in Greek script; follow same rules as for simple words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin: count syllables by vowels/diphthongs
rubrics_metrics.description: A Latin word has as many syllables as it has vowels or diphthongs (ae, au, oe, ei, eu, ui).

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin: divide before single consonant between vowels
rubrics_metrics.description: When a single consonant occurs between two vowels, divide before the consonant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cae-sar, me-ri-di-es.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin: divide before last consonant if multiple consonants
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of two or more consonants, divide before the last consonant, except in combinations mute+liquid and qu or gu.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: om-nis, scrip-tus, junc-tus (but: pa-tris, e-quus, lin-gua).

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin: compound words
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound words are separated first into component elements, and within each element earlier Latin rules apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ad-est, ab-rum-po, red-e-o, trans-i-go.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnote indices: superior figures preferred
rubrics_metrics.description: For reference indices, as a rule, use superior figures; only in special cases employ asterisks, daggers, etc.; index figures in the text should be placed after the punctuation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example placement shown; when figures are not used, sequence for symbols: * (asterisk), † (dagger), ‡ (double dagger), § (section mark), || (parallels), ¶ (paragraph mark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ibid.
rubrics_metrics.description: Where references to the same work follow each other closely and uninterruptedly, use 'Ibid.' instead of repeating the title. 'Ibid.' takes the place of as much of the previous reference as is repeated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Ibid.' should not ordinarily be used for the first footnote on a verso (left-hand) page; prefer repeating the title if short, or use loc. cit. or op. cit. Examples provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnotes to tables style
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnotes to tables, whether ruled or open, should be in 6-pt., and should invariably be placed at the foot of the table and not at the foot of the page. For reference indices in such cases use asterisks, etc., not superior figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (See related rule 232.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit author repetition in footnote
rubrics_metrics.description: If the author's name is given in the text in connection with a reference to, or a quotation from, his work, it should not be repeated in the footnote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: If text reads 'This theory is questioned by Herbert, as follows: "I cannot admit ..."*' then footnote is 'Laws of the Ancients, I, 153.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Place index figure after quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better to place the index figure in the text after the quotation than before it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration shown in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations and numeral styles in references
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily omit 'Vol.,' 'chap.,' and 'p.' in references to particular passages. Use Roman numerals (capitals) for Volume, Book, Part, and Division, except in references to ancient/classical authors when lower-case roman numerals should be used; Roman numerals (lower-case) for chapter and pages of introductory matter; Arabic numerals for number and text pages. Only use 'Vol.,' 'p.' etc., when confusion would arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In classical references use no comma between author's name and title of work, and no comma following the title unless 'Vol.,' 'p.' etc., are used. Examples given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date placement in periodical references
rubrics_metrics.description: The date of publication in a reference to a periodical should immediately follow the volume number, and should be put in parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See examples in manual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbering footnotes in linotype work
rubrics_metrics.description: In work set on the linotype machine footnotes should be numbered consecutively through an article (in a journal) or through a chapter (in a book) to save resetting in case of change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note exceptions (some journals number differently); see 'Hints to Authors and Editors.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: French/Belgian/Spanish particles
rubrics_metrics.description: A French, Belgian, or Spanish name preceded by 'le,' 'la,' 'l',' 'du,' or 'des' should be listed under the letters of the prefix in advance of the ordinary 'L' or 'D' list; if preceded by 'de' or 'd'' list under the first letter of the following word, placing the particle after initials or Christian name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Le Conte, John; La Noue, Francois de; L'Estrange, Sir Roger; Du Maurier, George; Des Essarts, Jean; d'Estrée, Gabrielle; Rambeau, Emile de. Note: If the particle is actually part of the surname, index under the particle (De Bey, De Quincey).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: German von
rubrics_metrics.description: German names preceded by 'von' should be indexed according to the initials of the name following the prefix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Sternthal, Max von; Goethe, J. W. von.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: M', Mac, Mc names
rubrics_metrics.description: Names beginning with 'M',' 'Mac,' or 'Mc,' with the following letter capitalized, should be indexed in that order, in advance of the ordinary 'M' list, each section arranged alphabetically according to the letters following the 'M',' 'Mac,' or 'Mc.' Names beginning with 'Mac' without a capitalized following letter should take their natural place in the 'M' list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: O', St., Van with capitalized following letter
rubrics_metrics.description: Names preceded by 'O',' 'St.,' or 'Van,' with the following letter capitalized, should be placed in advance of the 'O,' 'S,' or 'V' list and arranged alphabetically according to the letter following the particle. Names beginning with 'Van' without the following letter capitalized should take ordinary place in 'V' list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: names with connectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Names having two parts or firm names connected by 'and', '&', 'y', 'et', 'und', or 'e' should be listed according to the first letter of the name preceding the connective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Smith and Evans (under 'S'); Gomez y Pineda (under 'G'); Loubet et Meunier (under 'L').

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: hyphenated names
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenated names should be listed according to the name following the hyphen if English; according to the name preceding the hyphen if French.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Taylor, Henry Chandler- (for Henry Chandler-Taylor); Saint-Saëns, Charles Camille (for Charles Camille Saint-Saens).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: Umlaut treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: German names spelled with an Umlaut (Ä, Ö, Ü) should be indexed as if spelled with A, O, or U.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: cross-references
rubrics_metrics.description: On the subject of cross-references see rule 62 (referenced elsewhere in the manual).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tables: point sizes and setting for open/ruled tables
rubrics_metrics.description: In 11-pt. and 10-pt. matter open (unruled) tables should ordinarily be set in 9-pt. leaded; ruled, in 8-pt. solid. In 9-pt. matter both open and ruled tables should be set in 8-pt. solid. In 8-pt. matter open tables in 6-pt. leaded; ruled in 6-pt. solid. In 6-pt. matter both open and ruled tables in 6-pt. solid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is growing practice of using different type in tables for columns representing totals, averages, percentages; italic and black-face figures may be used to set off classes of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table captions and box-heads
rubrics_metrics.description: Captions for the columns of open tables and box-heads for ruled tables should ordinarily be set in 6-pt.; primary heads in caps and small caps, secondary in caps and lower-case. The 'stub' head should usually also be caps and small caps when small caps are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In multi-story box-heads follow the described sizing and case rules; see p.92 for illustrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table rule-to-matter spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: In ruled tables there should be at least two leads' space between the horizontal rules and the matter inclosed, and if practicable at least the equivalent of an en-quad of the type between the perpendicular rules and the matter inclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open tables: use of periods or leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: In open tables either periods, one em apart and aligned, or leaders, may be used between the columns; in ruled tables, in the 'stub,' leaders should usually be employed if room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A leader is type with dots (period leader) or short lines (hyphen leader) used to lead the eye across space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Columns of figures: blanks and alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: In columns of figures, to express a blank use leaders the width of the largest number in the column; center the figures in the column; if unequal digits leave more space on the left than right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For four digits use a 2-em leader; each em contains two dots; use not less than two dots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading-matter in ruled tables
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is reading-matter in the columns of a ruled table, it should be centered if possible; if any line runs over, use hanging indentation and align all on the left.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double rules at top of tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Double rules should be used at the top of all tables, but vertical double rules only when a table is doubled up on itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open vs ruled table decision by column count
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables of two columns only should be set as open; three or more as ruled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table numbering and headlines style
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Table I,' etc., in table headlines should ordinarily be set in caps of the type of the table; the descriptive line, if any, in caps and small caps of the same type. A single descriptive headline not preceded by number should be set in caps of the table type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specimen tables as illustration
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide specimen tables for illustration and follow demonstrated layouts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manual includes extensive specimen tables (Table I, Table II, etc.) to show practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point is basic typographical unit
rubrics_metrics.description: The point is the underlying unit of all typographical measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pica standard of measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard of measurement is the pica; a pica is twelve points (one-sixth of an inch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples showing lines set in various point sizes (12-pt, 11-pt, 10-pt, 9-pt, 8-pt, 7-pt, 6-pt, 5-pt) illustrate common sizes used in book composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roman type definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary type is called roman; to 'roman-quote' is to put in roman type between quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italic type definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Type with a sloping face is called italic or italics; indicated in manuscripts by a straight line under the word(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See p.123 for manuscript indications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bold-face definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Type with a heavy black face is called bold-face; indicated by a wavy line in manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See p.123 for indications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type anatomy terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical terms: the body of a type is called the shank; the upper surface bearing the character is the face; the part of the face projecting beyond the shank is the kern; the part of the shank projecting beyond the face is the shoulder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Font components
rubrics_metrics.description: A font is a complete assortment of a given size of type including large capitals (caps), small capitals (small caps), and lower-case letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manuscript indications: caps by three straight lines, small caps by two. Illustrations of caps, small caps, and lower case provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing terminology varies by setting system
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical names for spaces and methods of spacing depend on whether foundry (hand) type or machine-set type is used; monotype and linotype machines commonly used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different systems (monotype, linotype, foundry) have specific 'fixed' spaces and spreading mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotype spacing system
rubrics_metrics.description: In monotype composition the 'unit' system is used; there are 18 units in a quad. Fixed spaces of 6-unit (standard), 5-unit, 4-unit exist; during keyboard composition swelling/justifying spaces are used and spread to fill a line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operators strike keys indicating proper space when another word can't fit; all spaces in the line spread equally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linotype spacing system
rubrics_metrics.description: On the linotype machine the pica system of measurement is used; there are three fixed spaces: em-quad, en-quad, and thin (4-em) space. A space-band is used to spread spaces between 3-em and slightly larger than an en-quad. Very thin spaces must be set by hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Em/en/quads and dash/space definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: An em (or em-quad) is a square block (size varies with point); en-quad is half an em. Em- and en-dash widths correspond. Three-em, four-em, five-em spaces defined; hair-space defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of lines spaced with various quads and spaces and examples of em-dash and en-dash provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: General spacing: standard interword and punctuation spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Space evenly: standard line should have a 3-em space between words not separated by punctuation and after commas; an en-quad after semicolons and colons followed by a lower-case letter; two 3-em spaces after colons followed by a capital; an em-quad after periods and exclamation/interrogation points concluding a sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust spacing starting with commas and shoulder letters
rubrics_metrics.description: If necessary to reduce spacing in a line, begin with commas and letters of slanting form (large shoulder) to reduce; if increasing, begin with overlapping letters (with kerns protruding), straight-up-and-down letters, and points other than periods and commas (in that order).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion of 3-em and en-quad spaces in well-spaced line
rubrics_metrics.description: In a well-spaced line with a 3-em space between the majority of words, there should not be more than an en-quad between the rest; maintain this proportion when increasing or reducing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To justify a line is to adjust it by proper spacing to make it even.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid alternating extreme spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not follow an exceptionally thin-spaced line with an exceptionally wide-spaced one, or vice versa, if avoidable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not hair-space to avoid run-over
rubrics_metrics.description: Never hair-space, or em-quad, a line to avoid a run-over.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not space out paragraph last line
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not space out the last line of a paragraph allowing an indention of an em or more at the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal spacing around short words
rubrics_metrics.description: Short words like 'a,' 'an,' etc., should have the same space on each side.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thin space after special signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a thin space after §, %, and similar signs; before 'No.,' 'Ms.,' 'S.' and metric symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '§ 14. Be it further ordained ...'; 'pp. 10 ff.'; '16 cm.'

rubrics_metrics.name: No space between currency symbols and numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: In American and English sums of money no space is used between symbols ($, £, s., d.) and numerals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: $2.75; £10 3s. 2d.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing after numerals at lines/heads
rubrics_metrics.description: After Arabic and Roman numerals at the beginning of lines denoting subsections, use an en-quad. After Arabic and Roman numerals at the beginning of center-heads use an em-quad. Small-cap headings should have an en-quad between words; cap-and-small-cap and cap headings, two 3-em spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing for scripture references
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripture references should be spaced as: n Cor. 1:16-20; 2:5–3:12.

rubrics_metrics.name: No space between product letters and super/subscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Between letters forming products, and before superior figures/letters indicating powers and inferior figures/letters, ordinarily no space should be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example mathematical expression provided in manual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indentation sizes by measure and point size
rubrics_metrics.description: Indentation specifications: in measures less than 10 picas, indent all sizes 1 em; in measures 10–20 picas, various indents by point size (11-pt 1 em; 10-pt 1 em; 9-pt 1¼ em; 8-pt 1¼ em; 6-pt 2 ems); in 20–30 picas different indents; specific hanging indentation guidelines similarly enumerated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the recommended indention scheme for plain paragraphs and hanging indentions; use the table in the manual for precise values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indentation rules for poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: In poetry center the longest line and let indentation be governed by that; if longest line disproportionate, use an average. Where quotations from different poems vary slightly in verse line length, indent all alike. Indent according to rhymes and line length; align blank verse and consecutively rhyming lines; if rhymes alternate indent rhyming lines alike (e.g., lines 1 & 3 flush, lines 2 & 4 indented). If a line is disproportionately short indent it more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive illustrative examples of verse formatting provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer plain paragraphs; use hanging indentation sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary reading-matter, plain paragraphs are preferable. Use hanging indention when you wish to bring opening word(s) or paragraph number into relief or where a center-head makes more than three lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 284 for hanging indention details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leads: definition and standard thickness
rubrics_metrics.description: A lead is a strip of metal used to separate lines of type; the ordinary (standard) lead is 2 points thick. Matter with leads is called leaded; without, solid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This book is mostly set leaded; index and some paragraphs are set solid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slug definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A slug is a strip of metal, thicker than a lead, used in make-up of printed matter into pages; standard sizes are 6 and 12 points thick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center-head style and sizing
rubrics_metrics.description: A center-head is a headline placed at equal distances from both margins, usually set in caps or small caps; set them in roman or italic capitals two sizes smaller than the text type as a good working rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For multi-line center-heads use inverted pyramid for two or three lines or hanging indention for more than three lines; examples provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Side-head forms and capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: A side-head is a headline placed at the side of the page or column; it may be set as a separate flush line or run in. Side-heads are most frequently set in italics with only first word and proper names capitalized; sometimes in caps and small caps or bold-face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of various forms provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut-in head definition and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: A cut-in head is a head placed in a box cut into the side of the type-page, usually set in different type and as a rule placed under the first two lines of the paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example illustrated in manual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Box-head definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A box-head is a head for a column in a ruled table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (See table-related rules such as 242.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Running-heads: content and sizing
rubrics_metrics.description: A running-head is a headline placed at the top of each page, usually giving main title on the left-hand (verso) page and chapter or subdivision title on the right-hand (recto) page. Set running-heads in roman or italic capitals two sizes smaller than the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use running-heads to show title and chapter succinctly.
